claims.text: Approximately 6 hours of high-energy ball milling induces sufficient lattice strain and grain refinement in CoCrFeNiTi.
The milling-induced strain and grain refinement lower the barrier for an FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
SPS at 1000°C converts the milled CoCrFeNiTi material into a single-phase BCC structure.
At 1000°C, Ti-driven HCP precipitation remains kinetically suppressed in CoCrFeNiTi.
The mechanically alloyed starting powder has a nanocrystalline grain size below 20 nm.
Severe plastic deformation during milling produces a metastable FCC solid solution in CoCrFeNiTi.
SPS at 1000°C for 5–10 minutes can produce greater than 95% theoretical density.
The VEC and atomic-radius mismatch of the specified CoCrFeNiTi composition place it in a BCC stability region.
Rapid SPS heating and cooling suppress nucleation of Ti-rich HCP phases.
A high defect density and reduced grain size lower the activation energy of the FCC-to-BCC transition.
A temperature of 1000°C supplies sufficient diffusion for densification of ball-milled CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti-rich HCP precipitation typically reduces both ductility and hardness in cast alloys.
The proposed process will produce CoCrFeNiTi with porosity below 2%.
The proposed alloy will have significantly higher Vickers hardness than the cast baseline because of grain-boundary and solid-solution strengthening.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has low hardness and high porosity.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has a mixed FCC/BCC microstructure with possible Ti-rich HCP precipitates at grain boundaries.
Sintering above approximately 1050°C causes excessive grain growth.
Sintering above approximately 1050°C causes Ti-driven HCP precipitation, reverses hardness gains, and reduces ductility.
Oxygen or carbon contamination introduced during processing can stabilize HCP material and counteract formation of a single BCC phase.
Low-load Vickers hardness testing at 100 g isolates grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the FCC-to-BCC barrier thermodynamic, whereas the mediator and mechanism describe it as a kinetic or activation-energy barrier; these are conceptually distinct.

The boundary predicts that 1100°C should yield more HCP phase and lower hardness than 1000°C, but falsification criterion (3) treats that same observation as falsifying the hypothesis even though it would confirm the proposed boundary.
